title: God Remembered Noah — Remembrance, Wind, a Dove
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Last lesson ended in front of a door that had been shut. God was the one who shut it; outside, the waters were rising and rising, and inside there was nothing but silence. Through the whole of chapter 7, the text does not record a single word out of Noah's mouth.

The question this lesson puts to us is this: have you ever waited for something so long that you began to think God had probably forgotten? Noah was inside that ship for a year and ten days. Forty days of rain. A hundred and fifty days of water at its height. And after that, the waiting while the water went down an inch at a time. He could not get out, and he had no idea how much longer it would be.

Let me put the answer up front. The first sentence of chapter 8 is "God remembered Noah." And in the Bible, "to remember" has never meant "it suddenly came back to mind." It means "the time has come, and he has moved."
1. God Remembered — the Warmest Verb in the Bible
Verse 1: "God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship."

The word "remembered" is וַיִּזְכֹּר (*vayizkor*). Taken literally it is "he called to mind" — but in the Bible this word is almost never describing a function of the memory. It is describing the beginning of an action.

Look at every place it turns up in Scripture and you will see it. Genesis 19:29: "God remembered Abraham" — and then he sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow of Sodom. Genesis 30:22: "God remembered Rachel" — and then she conceived and bore a son. Exodus 2:24: "God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob" — and then came the exodus. Luke 23:42, where the criminal says, "Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom." He is not asking Jesus please not to forget him. He is asking Jesus to take him along.

So, brothers and sisters, "God remembered Noah" does not mean "God suddenly recalled that there was a boat out there somewhere." It means "God has begun to act on his behalf." And notice the clause the text adds: "all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship." Even the livestock are remembered. The list of those God remembers is longer than you imagine.

There is one more detail that matters a great deal: this sentence stands at the exact centre of the whole narrative. From 7:11, where the waters begin to rise, to 8:14, where the earth is completely dry, the hinge in the middle is this one line. Brothers and sisters, that longest stretch of waiting in your own life has a hinge in the middle of it too — and the hinge is not that you held on. It is that he remembered.
"God remembered Noah" — does that mean God had at some point forgotten him?

The Hebrew זָכַר (*zachar*) is not a function of the memory; it is "to act because of a covenant that has been made." So the weight of "remember" does not fall in the mind — it falls on the hands. The same word is used later of God remembering "his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob" (Exodus 2:24), and it is the word in the criminal's plea, "remember me." So this verse is not saying that God recalled something he had let slip. It is saying that God has begun to work. That matters enormously to anyone who is in the middle of waiting: when you feel as though God has forgotten you, most of the time it is not that he has forgotten — it is that his work has not yet reached the stage where you can see it. And what Scripture guarantees is this: when he remembers, the waters begin to go down.
The waters receded "continually", little by little. Why did God not simply drain them all at once?

Verse 3 of chapter 8 says the waters "continually receded from the earth"; verse 5 says they "receded continually"; and it is not until verse 14 that the earth is finally dry. From beginning to end it takes more than a year. The text spends a great deal of ink on that slow retreat, and the fact itself is the message: God's rescue is very often gradual. There are at least two practical reasons. First, the land had to recover to the point where it could be lived on again; drain it too fast and all you are left with is a field of mud. Second, the human heart needs time as well. What we ask for is usually an instant solution; what God does is usually a step-by-step restoration. So while you are waiting, the question to ask is not "why isn't this fixed yet?" but "what is he restoring during this stretch?"
2. God Made a Wind to Pass Over the Earth, and the Waters Subsided
The second half of verse 1: "and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided."
The word for "wind" is רוּחַ (*ruach*). Brothers and sisters, you know this word well by now — 1:2, "God's Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters", uses precisely the same word.

The author has done this on purpose. The first creation: a waste of water, the Spirit of God hovering over the surface of it, and then the dry land appearing. After the flood: a waste of water again, God making a רוּחַ pass over the earth, and then the tops of the mountains coming into view. Verse 13 says "the waters were dried up from the earth", and that is the picture of 1:9, "let the dry land appear", being played through a second time.

This is one of the most important pieces of logic in the whole Bible: salvation is not a repair job, it is a new creation. 2 Corinthians 5:17 says, "Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." And 2 Peter 3:5–7 sets the flood and the renewal at the end of the age side by side and speaks of them together. God's way of dealing with corruption has never been to patch up the old thing. It is to bring a new beginning up out of the water.

But notice that adverb: the waters subsided — continually. Little by little. Not drained overnight. Verse 3 says, "The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters receded." Verse 5 says, "The waters receded continually until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were visible."

Brothers and sisters, that word "continually" matters. God could have dried the whole earth with one sentence — it took him two words to make light. But he chose to let the waters go down slowly. Why? The text does not explain. What I have seen in pastoral work, though, tends to run like this: God shows his power in the places where things move fast, and he shapes our character in the places where things move slowly.

Verse 4 says, "The ship rested … on Ararat's mountains." The word "rested" is וַתָּנַח (*vatanach*), and its root נוּחַ is the very root of the name "Noah." So a Hebrew reader hears a pun at this point: the ship "Noah-ed" — it came to rest. After a whole year adrift, the ship finally settles down onto solid ground.
3. A Light from the Original: the Raven and the Dove
Verses 6 to 12 are the most vividly pictured passage in the chapter.

"At the end of forty days, Noah opened the window of the ship which he had made, and he sent out a raven." The word for "window" here is חַלּוֹן (*chalon*), and it is not the same word as the opening for light in 6:16. That one was the light-slit left in the hull when the ship was built; this is a window that can be opened. Brothers and sisters, that tiny difference of wording is saying something: at last he can open it a crack and take one look outside.

He sends the raven first. The raven, הָעֹרֵב (*ha'orev*), is listed in Leviticus 11:15 among the unclean birds, and it feeds on carrion. So it "went back and forth, until the waters were dried up from the earth" — that whole surface of water was covered with its food, and it had no need to come back.

Then he sends out the dove. The dove, הַיּוֹנָה (*hayonah*), is a clean bird, and it is the offering that the very poorest people of a later day could still afford to bring. Verse 9 says, "but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship."

Brothers and sisters — "He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship." That is the tenderest movement in the whole chapter. The clean bird would not settle on a surface of rotting water; she would rather come back. And there was a hand waiting for her at the window.

"He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship. The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf." A freshly plucked olive leaf — which means the water had dropped below the treetops, and that the tree was alive. One leaf, and it is the news of a whole world.

"He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove; and she didn't return to him any more." Brothers and sisters, in this short passage the phrase "waited yet another seven days" appears twice. Seven days each time. He was not flinging the window open every day in a fret. He waited to a rhythm.

This passage often gets misread as divination or superstition. It is nothing of the kind. Sending out birds to look for land was ordinary seamanship in that world — and more important still, he used the birds to read the water level, but he did not use the birds to decide when to go ashore. Verse 13 says the ground was dry, and he still stayed on board for almost two more months, until in verse 15 God spoke and said, "Go out of the ship."
Why a raven and a dove? What is the difference between the two birds?

The raven is an unclean bird that feeds on carrion, so it could go "back and forth" and live perfectly well — there was plenty out there for it to eat. The dove is a clean bird, and finding no place to set her foot, she flew back. The text passes no comment, but the contrast makes a striking picture: one and the same world, and some hearts can settle anywhere in it while other hearts cannot settle at all. And Noah's method is worth learning from. He waited seven days, then another seven, then another seven. He was not guessing; he was combining one tentative move after another with waiting. That is very practical for us when we are trying to judge the timing of something: when you are not sure, send out a dove, and then wait seven days.
"In her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf" — why is this verse so famous?

Because that leaf is the first piece of evidence that something new is already growing on the earth. It is not a report on how far the water has dropped; it is a report that life has come back. The olive tree goes on carrying the sense of peace and of anointing right through the Bible, and in the Gospels the dove becomes the picture of the Holy Spirit descending. So when age after age has taken this image as the sign of peace, there is a textual reason for it. What it means for us in practice is this: the first comfort God gives is very often not an announcement that "it is all over" — it is one small, freshly plucked leaf. You have to learn to recognise that leaf, and not discount it just because it looks too small to count.
4. The First Thing He Did After Leaving the Ship
Verses 15 and 16: "God spoke to Noah, saying, 'Go out of the ship, you, your wife, your sons, and your sons' wives with you.'"

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at what happens here. Verse 13 says "the waters were dried up from the earth", and that was the first day of the first month. Verse 14 says "the earth was dry", and that was the twenty-seventh day of the second month. Almost two whole months went by, and he did not go out. He waited for God to speak.
That is the hardest kind of obedience in the chapter. Not staying put while it is still dangerous — waiting when you can plainly see that you are free to go.
Then verse 20: "Noah built an altar to Yahweh, and took of every clean animal, and of every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on the altar."

Brothers and sisters, picture that moment. He has not set foot on soil in more than a year. There are eight people left in the whole world. Everything has to begin again from nothing — no house, no field, no neighbours. In that situation the most reasonable first move a person could make would be to throw up a shelter and find something to eat.

But the first thing he does is build an altar. And what he offers is "every clean animal" — precisely the ones God had specially commanded him in chapter 7 to take aboard in greater numbers. So those extra six had been prepared for this moment from the very beginning.

Verse 21: "Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake.'" And then verse 22: "While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease." Brothers and sisters, this is a guarantee of order given to the whole created world. The sun you watched come up this morning was that verse being honoured.
The first thing Noah did on leaving the ship was build an altar and offer sacrifice. Why not put up a house first?

Because the order a person puts things in decides what his life is going to look like from then on. The resources in his hands were tiny — seven pairs of each clean animal, and every one offered meant one fewer left; and he offered first. What that says is this: his first concern was not to make sure he could survive, but to settle whose he was. And the text goes straight on: "Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake.'" The new world begins at an altar. That is intensely practical for us: when you move into a new home, start a new company, step into a new stage of life — if the first thing you do is give thanks, give an offering, settle where you stand with God, then every decision that follows will be a different decision.
"The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth" — God says this after the flood. Does that not mean the flood washed nothing at all?

The flood did not change the human heart, and that is exactly what the text wants us to see. Genesis 6:5 says that "every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil"; Genesis 8:21 says "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth" — the same diagnosis. The difference lies in God's response. In chapter 6 the response is judgement; in chapter 8 the response is "I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake." That is to say: on one and the same fact, God made a decision of grace. This verse lays the whole Bible's problem and the whole Bible's answer out on the table at once — an outside force can clear away an environment, but it cannot renew a heart. Which is why, later on, there has to be One who says, "I will also give you a new heart", and why there has to be a cross.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "God remembered" as though God can forget. We have already seen it: this is action taken on the basis of a covenant, not a function of the memory. Psalm 121:4 says of him that he "will neither slumber nor sleep." If you preach it as God forgetting and then recalling, the congregation's confidence in God's faithfulness is discounted, and from then on their praying carries a certain anxiety in it — a feeling that they had better remind him.

The second is spending a whole sermon hunting for the ship on Ararat. An interest in archaeology is no bad thing, but it cannot take the place of this chapter's message. Whether or not that ship is ever found changes nothing at all about those two words, "God remembered." And let us be honest: at present there is no generally accepted evidence for it. There is no need, for the sake of effect in the pulpit, to preach a conjecture as a fact.

The third is preaching the "pleasant aroma" as though a human sacrifice can change God's mind. Psalm 50:12–13 says plainly that if God were hungry he would not need to tell us. And notice the wording of verse 21 — "said in his heart." That is a declaration God makes on his own initiative; he was not talked round by the smell of roasting meat. Preach it as a transaction and you have turned sacrifice into a bribe.

The fourth is preaching that the waters went down and never getting as far as the altar. The altar in verse 20 is the summit of the chapter. If all you preach is "just get through it", what the congregation learns is a technique for enduring, not a heart for worship. The test is this: does this sermon of yours teach the congregation to grit their teeth, or to worship?

The fifth is reading 8:21, "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth", as a piece of gloomy pessimism. Set it beside 6:5: the same verdict is used earlier to bring the flood, and later to make a covenant never to bring one again. The same reason, and God's dealing with it has been turned completely around. The real message of this verse is that the flood proved that swapping in a new batch of people does not work. What humanity needs is not one more fresh start; it is to be born again.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I am in a very long wait — waiting for an illness to lift, waiting for a child to turn around, waiting for a door to open at work — and I keep feeling that God has stopped bothering. How do I tell? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives us two very practical clues. The first clue is that word "continually." God's way of working is very often not an overnight reversal; it is a retreat of an inch at a time. So "it is not better yet" is not the same thing as "he has not moved." Here is something you can practise: every month, write down one thing that is a little better than it was the month before, however small. You will discover that the water really is going down. The second clue is rhythm. Noah "waited yet another seven days"; he was not throwing the window open in a fret every day. In a long wait, give yourself a rhythm — a fixed time in the Scriptures, a fixed gathering, a fixed habit of telling one person the truth. That rhythm will hold you up through the stretch of days whose length you cannot know.

The second question: Chinese people set great store by *fou ji tai lai* — when misfortune reaches its limit, good fortune turns back — and by *feng shui lun liu zhuan*, fortune takes its turn on the wheel. Is that the same as what chapter 8 is saying? My answer is: the shape is similar, the ground underneath is entirely different. The ground under "when misfortune reaches its limit, good fortune turns back" is the cycle — once things are as bad as they can get they naturally turn upward — and that is a trust placed in a regularity. The ground under chapter 8 is a Person: God remembered Noah. The first is probability; the second is relationship. Inside suffering that difference is enormous: a person who believes in the cycle can only wait, while a person who believes there is a God who remembers him can ask. And notice verse 22 — what God guarantees, "seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night", is exactly what our own tradition calls the turning of the four seasons. Scripture does not deny that regularity. Scripture simply tells you that the regularity has an Author, and that he keeps his covenant.
How do you tell waiting apart from procrastination? I am always saying that I am waiting for God's timing.

Three very practical tests. First, waiting has actions in it. Noah was waiting — but he opened the window, sent out birds, watched, kept a record of the days. Procrastination does nothing at all. Second, waiting has content. He knew what he was waiting for: for the ground to be dry. Procrastination usually cannot say what it is waiting for. Third, waiting is willing to be examined. Tell your spiritual companion what you are waiting for, and let him ask you about it. If you do not dare let anyone know, it is most likely procrastination. The last verse of chapter 8 says, "While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease" — God's rhythm never stops running. Waiting means joining his rhythm; it does not mean pressing pause on your days.
7. Living 321 Out — Build the Altar First, the House Afterwards
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the first thing Noah did on leaving the ship was to build an altar and offer sacrifice. And the Lord Jesus lived his whole life the same way round: he offered himself first and then went to work. He was baptised, he fasted, and only then did he begin to preach; he went out to a lonely place to pray while it was still dark, and only then did he heal the sick and drive out demons. My role model is very concrete: the first movement after receiving something is worship, not celebration.

The Bible is my standard — the most piercing line of the standard in this chapter is in verse 21: "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." That is God's assessment of the human being, and having said it, he still goes on to make his covenant. A standard is not there only to make demands of people; it also tells us how much God knows about us while he goes on loving us. He has not overestimated you. He chose you anyway.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the wind in verse 1 is the same word as the one that hovered over the face of the waters at creation. Brothers and sisters, the new beginning in your life and the first beginning of the world are the work of one and the same Person. And his way of working is very often "continually", not "at once".

Let Jesus be King — the waters had gone down, and Noah still did not open the door himself; he waited until verse 15, when God said, "Go out of the ship." Letting Jesus be King means letting him have the last word even on "now is the time." Brothers and sisters, the place where we most often step out of line is not direction; it is timing. We agree that we ought to go. We just do not agree that we ought to wait.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — look at the subject of the sentences right through this chapter: God remembered, God made a wind to pass over, God spoke, Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma, Yahweh said in his heart. The human being does three things: he opens a window, he sends out birds, he builds an altar. And that third thing is precisely the act of handing the glory back.

Establish God's system — in verse 22 God promises that the seasons will not cease, and that is an order laid down for the whole created world. Brothers and sisters, the rhythm of God's kingdom is predictable, it is faithful, and it does not shift about with anybody's mood. So to establish God's system is to bring that kind of reliability into my own home: what I said stands, I turn up at the time we agreed, I do the thing I promised. The first way a child ever learns what God's faithfulness is like is usually whether or not his father keeps his word.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We often say, "change the mindset and you change the life" — and this chapter adds a very sober footnote to that. Genesis 8:21 says that after the flood the evil in the human heart had not shifted by so much as an inch. Swapping in a new set of people does not work, and changing the environment does not work either. So if the renewing of the mindset is not joined to the cross and to new birth, the most it can ever amount to is a change of vocabulary. Real change is not that I have finally thought it through; it is that Christ lives in me.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "God Remembered"
Brothers and sisters, the same sentence — "God remembered Noah" — falls into four different kinds of heart, and what each one hears is completely different.

The proud heart says: "Of course God remembers me; I have been faithful all along." This heart has read remembrance as repayment. Brothers and sisters, look at the setting of verse 1: inside that ship Noah did nothing whatever, and the text does not record one word he said. God remembered him not because he held on, but because God remembered what God himself had said.

The fearful heart says: "What if he misses me out?" This heart repeats the same request over and over in prayer, afraid it has not been said clearly enough or often enough. To a heart like that I want to say: Isaiah 49:15 says, "Can a woman forget her nursing child … Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!" And the next verse says, "Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands." You do not have to remind him.

The ashamed heart says: "Someone like me — I don't suppose it will ever be my turn to be remembered." Brothers and sisters, look at who is on the list in verse 1: Noah, and all the animals, and all the livestock. Even the livestock are on that list. It is not a list ordered by contribution. It is a list ordered by grace.

The wounded heart says: "He remembered Noah. So what about the thing I have been waiting for?" This heart may have been waiting for years. I am not going to hand you a cheap answer. I only want to point out two facts in this chapter. First, the sentence "God remembered" stands at the very centre of the story — which means that before it ever arrives there are seven whole chapters of water. Second, the waters "receded continually", which means the process of going down looks, while you are inside it, exactly like nothing going down at all. You may be inside that word "continually" right now.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, keep a water-level record. Pick one thing you are currently waiting for, and write down every scrap of progress from the last three months, however small. You need to see that word "continually" with your own eyes.

Second, give your waiting a rhythm. Noah "waited yet another seven days." This week, set yourself a rhythm: a fixed time in the Scriptures, a fixed day on which you do not look at the thing that is eating at you, a fixed appointment to tell one person the truth. Rhythm is what will carry you through the long stretch.

Third, build the altar first and the house afterwards. If something good happens this week — the interview went through, the report came back, a relationship eased — then before you tell anybody at all, spend three minutes giving thanks. Change the order a little and the heart changes with it.

Fourth, practise moving only after he has spoken. Find one thing you are already free to act on but are not yet sure is what he wants, and deliberately wait three more days, praying about it every one of them. The ground was dry, and Noah still waited two months.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: there is a line in the Bible that says "God remembered Noah", and "remember" in the Bible does not mean calling something to mind, it means putting out a hand; at that point he had already been on board for over a year with nothing he could do about anything; so here is what I learned — silence does not mean you have been forgotten, and the water goes down slowly, it is not drained overnight.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I am not getting through this silence by holding on under my own strength; I am being carried by a God who has never once stopped remembering me.
I declare that I accept the word "continually"; the work he does in the slow places is every bit as real as the work he does in the fast ones.
I declare that even "the time has come" is his to say; I will not open the door myself.
I declare that after I receive something, my first movement will be to build an altar, not to celebrate.
This week we are told to "recognise that small leaf" — but in the situation I am in right now I honestly cannot see anything improving at all. What then?

Let me say something honest first: there are seasons when you simply cannot see anything, and the text does not ask anyone to pretend otherwise. The first time Noah sent the dove out she came back with nothing — empty, not a thing in her mouth — and that day is written down in the Bible too. So there are two things to do. First, lower the bar to this: is there one small thing still here today? A meal. One person who is still willing to listen to you. One verse that has not been taken away from you. Write it down. It does not have to be an improvement; it only has to be still here. Second, do not do the counting on your own. Find a companion, and every day send each other one thing that is still here today. And if you have gone a long stretch unable to feel any hope at all, and it is affecting your sleep and your appetite, please go to a pastor, and seek professional help as well — that is not a shortage of faith; that is taking care of yourself.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, I want it to be the hand that reaches out in verse 9.
"The dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him … He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship."

The whole world was water, and there was not one patch of dry ground to stand on. The clean bird flew all day, grew tired, and came back. And at the window there was a hand waiting, and it took her in.

Brothers and sisters, this week you may be that dove. You flew out, you tried hard, and you could not find anywhere to set your foot down. You feel that you have failed, and so you are too ashamed to come back.

Look carefully at that hand. The text does not say Noah rebuked her for failing to find land, and it does not say she ought to have flown a while longer. The text says only this: "He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship."

And thousands of years later the Lord Jesus says, in Matthew 11:28, "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest." Rest — that is the very root of the name "Noah."

The focus is not on how long I have waited, not on whether this flight of mine came back with anything to show, and not on when the water will finally be gone. The focus is on Jesus — he is the God who remembers us, and he is the hand reaching out at the window. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to settle down inside a long wait, and on the day the waters go down, to build an altar first. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ The original behind "remember" means "to act because of a covenant". If you change it from "calling to mind" to "putting out a hand", how does that change the way you pray?
2. ★★ The waters receded "continually", and it took more than a year from beginning to end. Why did God not drain them all at once?
3. ★ The raven went back and forth; the dove found no place to rest her foot and came back. What does the contrast between those two birds bring to your mind?
4. ★★ The first thing done on leaving the ship was to build an altar. If it had been a house first instead, how would the days that followed have been different?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can afford to wait; I can work the timing out for myself), fearful (what if the water comes back?), ashamed (I have waited so long that I no longer dare tell anyone), wounded (there was a time when I thought God had forgotten me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something you have been waiting on for a long time? How do you tell whether you are waiting or procrastinating?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The small leaf I saw this week was …" And if you genuinely cannot see one, say so honestly.
9. ★★ What kind of "altar" will you build this week for the stage you are in — one concrete act of giving thanks first, giving an offering first, entrusting it first?

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch long waiting and long disappointment. If someone cannot name a single leaf, do not rush to find one for him; sit with him a while first. Where a long-standing sense of hopelessness is involved and it is affecting sleep and appetite, follow up privately after the meeting and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home this week, is there something you mean to "offer up first" rather than take hold of first? Name it.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, which matter will you hand over to God before you act on it?
12. ★★★ The one-leaf-a-day practice: this week, before you sleep, write down one thing that is still here today. Say where you are going to write it.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and every day this week send each other one thing that is still here today. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, when the Bible says "God remembered", it does not mean he called something to mind; it means he put out his hand. Second, the water went down slowly — a whole year of it. Third, so I have learned, in days when things are only getting better slowly, to count that small leaf first. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the "altar" you are going to build this week, and who you are going to tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to let us recognise, while we still cannot see anything, that he has already put out his hand.
